title: Palmyra
wiki_lead:
Palmyra is an ancient city in central Syria. Located in the eastern part of the Levant, archaeological finds around the site date back to the Neolithic period, and documents first mention the city in the early second millennium BC. Palmyra changed hands on a number of occasions between different empires before becoming a subject of the Roman Empire in the first century AD.
The city grew wealthy from trade caravans; the Palmyrenes became renowned as merchants who established colonies along the Silk Road and operated throughout the Roman Empire. Palmyra's wealth enabled the construction of monumental projects, such as the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel, and the distinctive tower tombs. Ethnically, the Palmyrenes combined elements of Amorites, Arameans, and Arabs. Socially structured around kinship and clans, Palmyra's inhabitants spoke Palmyrene Aramaic, a variety of Western Middle Aramaic, while using Koine Greek for commercial and diplomatic purposes. The Hellenistic period of West Asia influenced the culture of Palmyra, which produced distinctive art and architecture that combined different Mediterranean traditions. The city's inhabitants worshiped local Semitic, Mesopotamian, and Arab deities.
By the third century, Palmyra had become a prosperous regional center. It reached the apex of its power in the 260s, when the Palmyrene King Odaenathus defeated the Sasanian emperor Shapur I. The king was succeeded by queen regent Zenobia, who rebelled against Rome and established the Palmyrene Empire. In 273, Roman emperor Aurelian levelled the city, which was later restored by Diocletian at a reduced size. The Palmyrenes converted to Christianity during the fourth century and to Islam in the centuries following the conquest by the seventh-century Rashidun Caliphate, after which the Palmyrene and Greek languages were replaced by Arabic.
Before 273 AD, Palmyra enjoyed autonomy and was attached to the Roman province of Syria, having its political organization influenced by the Greek city-state model during the first two centuries AD. The city became a Roman colonia during the third century, leading to the incorporation of Roman governing institutions, before becoming a monarchy in 260. Following its razing in 273, Palmyra became a minor center under the Byzantines and later empires. Its destruction by the Timurids in 1400 reduced it to a small village. Under French Mandatory rule in 1932, the inhabitants were moved into the new village of Tadmur, and the ancient site became available for excavations. During the Syrian civil war in 2015, the Islamic State captured Palmyra and destroyed large parts of the ancient city, which was recaptured by the Syrian Army on 2 March 2017. It was then captured by the Syrian Free Army after the fall of the Assad government in December 2024.

Etymology
Records of the name "Tadmor" date from the early second millennium BC; 18th-century BC tablets from Mari written in cuneiform record the name as "Ta-ad-mi-ir", while Assyrian inscriptions of the 11th century BC record it as "Ta-ad-mar". Palmyrene inscriptions themselves showed two variants of the name; TDMR (i.e., Tadmar) and TDMWR (i.e., Tadmor). The etymology of the name is unclear; the standard interpretation, supported by Albert Schultens, connects it to the Semitic word for "date palm", tamar (תמר), thus referring to the palm trees that surrounded the city.
The Greek name Παλμύρα (Latinized Palmyra) was first recorded by Pliny the Elder in the first century AD. It was used throughout the Greco-Roman world. It is generally believed that "Palmyra" derives from "Tadmor" and linguists have presented two possibilities; one view holds that Palmyra was an alteration of Tadmor. grok_lead: Palmyra, anciently known as Tadmor, is an oasis city and archaeological site located in the Syrian Desert approximately 215 kilometers northeast of Damascus, which functioned as a crucial caravan station facilitating trade between the Roman Empire and eastern regions including Persia, India, and China. First attested in Mesopotamian records from the second millennium BCE, it developed into a prosperous urban center blending Parthian, Roman, Arabian, and local Semitic influences, evidenced by its monumental architecture such as colonnaded streets, temples, and tower tombs. Under Roman control from the mid-first century CE, Palmyra's wealth from silk and spice routes supported a merchant aristocracy and distinct religious practices, reaching its zenith in the third century when Septimius Odaenathus and his widow Zenobia expanded its influence into a breakaway empire encompassing Syria, Egypt, and parts of Asia Minor, briefly defying Roman dominance. This challenge prompted Emperor Aurelian's campaign in 272â273 CE, which sacked the city, massacred much of its population, and dismantled its imperial structures, though it later revived modestly before declining with shifting trade paths. Rediscovered in the early modern era, Palmyra's ruins were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980 for their testimony to ancient cosmopolitanism, but the site's integrity was severely compromised during ISIS occupation in 2015â2017, when militants demolished temples, the Tetrapylon, and other monuments as part of ideological iconoclasm, alongside public executions in its theater. Post-conflict assessments confirm extensive but not total loss, with ongoing international efforts focused on documentation and partial reconstruction amid Syria's instability.
